subject: statistics for science course with STAN

messages.author: 7b2fb40653accdcf
messages.subject: statistics for science course with STAN
parts:
I had an opportunity to teach a course titled 'Statistics for Science' this semester (24 undergraduates, mostly juniors and seniors, 50% computer science/engineering majors with a few math, environmental science, and bio majors).   Topics included the usual survey of estimation and linear models (regression, ANOVA, ANCOVA).

I decided to take a chance and go all in with STAN (via rstan) as the default software and Bayesian as the dominant paradigm (despite the fact that I was trained as a frequentist in the 1970's). 

Students used their own computers (65% mac, the rest windows).  Aside from a few headaches getting things to run on windows (which the CS students took as a challenge and for the most part quickly resolved) everything worked great and students generally liked the course. 

I think this audience would have tuned out a more traditional approach very quickly.

Thank you for STAN!

messages.author: 7b2fb40653accdcf
messages.subject: Re: statistics for science course with STAN
parts:
Hi  Ben.

I have to admit I just learned about rstanarm this week (at a STAN meetup in Boston).  I learned about Richard McElreath's rethinking package a couple of weeks ago (I used two of the code examples from his book).

I have taught this course a number of times using R and, and more recently somef JAGS, but with a more frequentist flavor and more theory.  I'ts been hard to keep  the CS students engaged, but they were very enthusiastic this time around.   

I decided to post because at the meetup Jonah said he was glad to hear that someone had used STAN in a course and it worked well. There was some discussion about the scarcity of courses using STAN and I thought it might encourage others to use it.

Gene
